data.text/markdown:
Downloading the whole XIT001 corpus

Notebook 01 pulled one prefecture-quarter at a time. To train anything we want the lot on disk, fetched once, so every later experiment is an offline operation on a local file. The good news is that "the lot" is small:
Rows nationwide, 2005 Q3 – 2026 Q1 ~6.4M
Requests needed 3,901 (47 prefectures × 83 quarters)
Wall time, sequential ~12 min
On disk, parquet + zstd ~80 MB
That last number is why this is easy. The same data as JSON would be ~4.5 GB; parquet's dictionary encoding compresses these highly repetitive strings about 65×. There is no need to sample, scope to a region, or build incremental-update machinery — just download everything and filter locally. This notebook stops at the raw download. Responses land on disk exactly as the API returned them: every value still a string, 9999 sentinels intact, 戦前 intact, both price sources mixed together. Cleaning is deliberately a separate step, so that a change of mind about cleaning never costs a re-download. In particular there is no priceClassification filter, so both populations are kept — 不動産取引価格情報 (the buyer survey, 2005 Q3+) and 成約価格情報 (REINS broker data, 2021 Q1+) — with PriceCategory preserved so they can be separated later.

The request grid

One request is one (prefecture, year, quarter) cell. Two things fix the shape of the grid: Prefecture is the right granularity. XIT001 accepts area (prefecture), city or station, and a prefecture query returns everything the municipality queries would. Checked directly: Tottori 2024 Q1 returns 381 rows via area=31, and 381 rows via summing all 19 of its city= calls. Fetching by municipality would mean ~1,900 requests per quarter instead of 47, for identical data. The series starts at 2005 Q3, not 2005 Q1. Asking for 2005 Q1 or Q2 returns HTTP 400 ('year'、'quarter'の組み合わせが不正です。). The grid skips them rather than fetching and failing.

Three response shapes, not one

This is the part that a naive loop gets wrong. XIT001 answers in three different ways, and only the first is a success:
Status Body Means What to do
200 {"status":"OK","data":[…]} rows write them
404 {"message":"検索結果がありません。"} legitimately empty write an empty file
400 {"message":{"insufficient":…}} bad parameters raise — the grid has a bug
Note the 404. A prefecture-quarter with no recorded transactions is not an error, but it does not come back as {"data": []} either — it comes back as a 404 with no data key at all. Notebook 01's client calls raise_for_status() and would blow up on those; it only gets away with it because it never asks for an empty cell. Caching the empties matters too. If an empty cell writes nothing, every re-run re-requests every empty cell forever, and "resume" stops being cheap. Everything else — timeouts, 429, 5xx — is transient and gets retried with backoff.

Where it goes on disk

One file per grid cell, named {year}Q{quarter}_{area}.parquet. The presence of the file is the cache: the loop skips any cell that already has one, which makes the download interruptible and a resume nearly free.

Why not Hive partitioning

The obvious layout is year=2024/quarter=1/area=13/…, which readers understand natively. It is a trap here. Partition values are type-inferred, so area=01 reads back as the integer 1 — silently destroying the leading zero on prefecture codes 01–09, from Hokkaido through Fukui. You would not notice until a join against municipality codes quietly dropped nine prefectures. Flat filenames plus explicit string columns avoid the whole problem. The partitioning would have bought query pruning, which is worth nothing on an 80 MB dataset that reads in about two seconds. So each file carries three ingest-metadata columns — _area, _year, _quarter, underscore-prefixed to distinguish them from the API's own 29 fields, all stored as strings.

Running it

A twelve-minute loop needs care in a reactive notebook: marimo re-runs a cell whenever anything it depends on changes, and a download that restarts every time you touch a slider would be unusable. The button below is the guard — the loop body runs only when it is clicked, never on a reactive re-run. One refinement on pure skip-if-exists: the most recent four quarters are always re-fetched. Recent quarters keep gaining rows for months as survey responses trickle in, so a cached copy of a fresh quarter goes stale in a way that a settled quarter never does.

Checking what landed

Reading the flat tree back is one call. The per-year counts are the real integrity check — they should show the scheme ramping up through 2006, settling around 70–80k rows a quarter, then jumping in 2021 when the REINS contract-price feed switches on.

What's next

The corpus on disk is deliberately raw, which means every trap from notebook 01 is still in it. The next step is a proper cleaning layer, and this is the list it has to deal with:
  • Everything is a string, with "" for missing rather than null.
  • Area / TotalFloorArea of 9999 is a censored value meaning "≥5,000 m²", not a measurement.
  • BuildingYear of 戦前 — a literal string sitting in a numeric field.
  • Period needs parsing into a sortable year/quarter.
  • Two populations in one file. PriceCategory separates the buyer survey from the REINS broker data. They are not interchangeable: for Tokyo condos in 2024 the broker rows show a 46% higher median price but a 12% lower median price per m², because they sample larger units. They also populate different fields — CoverageRatio is 99% filled in the survey data and 18% in REINS — so a model trained on the pool can infer the data source and use it as a shortcut.
  • 2006 is thin (~19k rows in Q2 against ~64k in 2007) because the scheme was still ramping up. Probably worth dropping.
That work belongs in src/jp_housing_pred/, as an importable module rather than notebook cells — which is the next thing to build.
